catalog_quote: 2.4 Stress. Most unaffixed words consist of one or two syllables. The stress on a two syllable word generally falls on the first syllable. (56) /tɔwuŋ/ [ˈtɔ.wuŋ] 'egg' ... There is usually equal stress on both syllables when they each have the same vowel. (57) /ʌpmʌk/ [ˈʌp.ˈmʌk] 'cough' ... The weight of a syllable may also affect the stress on a word. The lightest of syllables are those with the short vowel, [ɨ]. If this occurs in the initial syllable the stress occurs on the next syllable as in (58). When the initial vowel is [ɪ], also very light, the first two syllables receive equal stress as in (59). (58) /bitsɛp/ [ᵐbɨ.ˈtsʲɛp] 'time' (59) /tsiwet/ [ˈtsɪ.ˈɥet] 'pit-pit' ... If the first syllable is a single vowel the first two syllables receive equal stress if the second syllable is CV or CVC as in (60). audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the scan we hold at the stated pages (book 17-19 = PDF 25-27; p.18 image read directly). (2) The source is the language's sole reference grammar (1994, vii+259 pp, first-hand SIL fieldwork) with a dedicated stress section; Glottolog's four descriptive refs reduce to this one work plus a phrase book, and a web search (SIL archives, TWU repository, Wikipedia/Glottolog trails) turned up no later or instrumental treatment. (3) The authors' own 1992 OPD sheet, downloaded now from the Internet Archive, independently states 'The stress is predictable and falls most often to the first syllable', consistent with the initial-default-plus-light-vowel-exceptions reading coded as weight-hedged (left edge, full-vs-reduced-vowel weight class); Moe's Domung thesis reads Spaulding the same way. The only unheld item is the 1988 Phonology Essentials manuscript (offline, same authors

sources.quote: Second-hand summary of Spaulding 1994: 'Nankina [nnk] ... Variable accent system: Accent typically falls on the first syllable of bisyllabic words; the system is complex and varies by syllable weight, vowel quality, and reduplication status. Some syllables receive equal degrees of accent but the final syllable is rarely accented.' Lists Spaulding 1988 Phonology Essentials and 1992 OPD as the only other Nankina phonology sources.

Low priority: same authors, superseded by the held 1994 volume.
